title: The Internal vs. External Audience
author: Ollie Lovell
summary: This short, confessional essay by educator and researcher Ollie Lovell examines the distinction between writing, speaking, or acting for an external audience (to gain approval, kudos, or recognition) versus an internal audience (one's own values, integrity, and the spirit of inquiry). Using two personal examples -- signing a house contract to impress school friends, and writing a social media post designed to make someone look bad rather than to encourage reflection -- Lovell argues that most modern discourse is performative rather than exploratory because participants are primarily playing to an external audience. He finds intellectual support in Ezra Pound's reply to Whitman: the only 'great audience' worth serving is the spirit of the art itself -- the eternal rather than the vulgo. The practical conclusion is a personal resolve to keep better counsel with his own values when writing in all forms.
points: * The common thread Lovell identifies across his poor decisions is audience: when he pictured external observers (old school mates, Twitter followers) during decision-making, the decision deteriorated; when he kept counsel with his internal values, it didn't. * The social media post example is the sharpest illustration: he was 'on the right side' of the argument but the framing was wrong -- he was calling the person out to gain kudos from observers rather than calling them in to encourage reflection, making the action performative rather than truth-seeking. * The Pound/Whitman distinction provides the philosophical core: Whitman argued that great poetry requires great audiences (external); Pound replied that the only true great audience is the spirit of irony and destiny sitting beside the artist (internal) -- to please the public is one thing, to keep council with the eternal is another. * The diagnosis of modern debate is precise: we write not for truth or progress but for an audience, turning exchanges into performances rather than explorations -- a pattern that explains why debate rarely changes minds and frequently degrades into posturing. * The personal resolve is modest and practical: endeavor to explore rather than perform, to write primarily for the internal audience of one's own values and inquiry rather than to capture the approval of the external one.
quotes: This is fundamentally what I think is the problem with almost every modern debate. We write not for truth or progress, but instead for an audience. Exchanges become performative, rather than exploratory.

As I wrote it, I wasn't imagining how my words might influence the perspective of the person I was writing to; I was instead imagining who might read it, and how I might gain kudos from those people for saying the right thing.

Ezra Pound put it more poetically than I ever could: 'It is true that the great artist always has a great audience, even in his lifetime; but it is not the vulgo but the spirits of irony and of destiny and of humor, sitting beside him.'

In his reply, Pound cleverly re-defines 'great audience' as 'the vulgo' (to oversimplify, 'the people') and states that to him, the only true 'great audience' is the spirit of poetry itself. To please the public is one thing, to keep council with that which is eternal is another thing entirely.

I hope that I have built my career on a spirit of inquiry. This week, I feel like I mimicked a spirit of inquiry to score points. And so, I add another mistake to the tally. I will endeavour to continue to explore rather than perform.
